cards.front: What does a sequencer report, and why is that not yet a genome?
cards.back: It reports reads, the base sequences of single DNA fragments. Reporting a base is not locating it in a genome.
cards.quote: a sequencer reports reads, the base sequences of single DNA fragments, and reporting a base is not locating it in a genome.

cards.front: State the one idea of the sequencing and genomes lesson.
cards.back: Genome results depend on what each read records and where it fits.
cards.quote: Genome results depend on what each read records and where it fits.

cards.front: In a Sanger reaction, what is the primer for?
cards.back: It is short DNA that pairs with the template and gives the polymerase a 3' end to extend.
cards.quote: a short primer (DNA that pairs with the template and gives the polymerase a 3' end to extend)
cards.section: Reading DNA one base at a time: Sanger's stopped copies

cards.front: In the classical Sanger method, how were the four bases read from the products?
cards.back: Four tubes each held one kind of ddNTP. The radioactive fragments ran in four lanes of a gel that separates pieces differing by one nucleotide, so band order gave base order.
cards.quote: four tubes each held one kind of ddNTP, and the radioactive fragments ran in four lanes of a gel
cards.section: Reading DNA one base at a time: Sanger's stopped copies

cards.front: Why does a dideoxynucleotide stop a growing DNA chain after the polymerase adds it?
cards.back: It lacks the 3' hydroxyl, so the next nucleotide has nothing to bond to.
cards.quote: A ddNTP lacks the 3' hydroxyl that the next nucleotide must bond to
cards.section: Reading DNA one base at a time: Sanger's stopped copies

cards.front: In Sanger sequencing, shortest to longest fragment spells the new strand 5' to 3'; the template is its {{c1::reverse complement}}.
cards.quote: Shortest to longest spells the new strand 5' to 3'; the template is its reverse complement.
cards.section: Reading DNA one base at a time: Sanger's stopped copies

cards.front: A Sanger detector reports the shortest fragments in order as T, G, G and A. What are the new strand and its template, each written 5' to 3'?
cards.back: New strand 5'-TGGA-3'. The template is antiparallel and complementary: 3'-ACCT-5', which is 5'-TCCA-3'. Complementing without reversing gives the template backwards.
cards.quote: Shortest to longest spells the new strand 5' to 3'; the template is its reverse complement.
cards.section: Reading DNA one base at a time: Sanger's stopped copies

cards.front: How did later Sanger methods get all four bases into one reaction and read them?
cards.back: Each terminator carries its own fluorescent dye. A capillary sorts fragments by size while a detector reads each colour.
cards.quote: Later versions give each terminator its own fluorescent dye, so one reaction holds all four, and a capillary sorts fragments by size while a detector reads each colour.
cards.section: Reading DNA one base at a time: Sanger's stopped copies

cards.front: What are the main limits of a Sanger read?
cards.back: Each reaction reads one region, commonly up to about 800 to 1,000 bases, and the first few dozen bases are often poor.
cards.quote: each reaction reads one region, commonly up to about 800 to 1,000 bases, and the first few dozen bases are often poor.
cards.section: Reading DNA one base at a time: Sanger's stopped copies

cards.front: In Illumina short-read sequencing, how does a reversible terminator let the machine read one base per cycle?
cards.back: It blocks the 3' end, so only one dye-carrying nucleotide adds. Imaging reads it, then cleaving off the dye and block restores the 3' hydroxyl for the next cycle.
cards.quote: cleaving off the dye and the block regenerates the 3' hydroxyl for the next cycle.
cards.section: Reading millions at once, short and long

cards.front: What does a paired-end read give that a single-end read does not?
cards.back: Two short sequences from both ends of one fragment, plus roughly how far apart they lie.
cards.quote: Reading each fragment from both ends, a paired-end read, gives two short sequences and roughly how far apart they lie.
cards.section: Reading millions at once, short and long

cards.front: What is the trade-off between short reads and long reads?
cards.back: Short reads give many accurate bases per run but cannot span long repeats. Long reads span most of them, though the largest repeat arrays still need ultra-long reads and special assembly.
cards.quote: short reads give many accurate bases per run but cannot span long repeats; long reads span most of them
cards.section: Reading millions at once, short and long

cards.front: In de novo assembly, what are contigs and what do scaffolds add?
cards.back: Contigs are continuous consensus sequences joined by read overlaps. Scaffolds place contigs in order and orientation, with estimated gaps between them.
cards.quote: Scaffolds place contigs in order and orientation, with estimated gaps between them.
cards.section: Coverage and assembly: two different limits

cards.front: How is mean coverage C calculated from the number of reads N, read length L and genome size G?
cards.back: C = N x L / G: all bases read, spread over the genome. Example: 1,000 reads of 100 bases on 10,000 bases gives 10-fold.
cards.section: Coverage and assembly: two different limits

cards.front: How many 100-base reads give 25-fold mean coverage of a 2-megabase genome, assuming random, usable reads?
cards.section: Coverage and assembly: two different limits

cards.front: At a fixed mean coverage and genome size, what happens to the number of reads needed if read length doubles?
cards.back: It halves, because N = C x G / L. Doubling L from 150 to 300 bases halves 6.2 x 10^8 reads to 3.1 x 10^8 in the 30-fold human example.
cards.quote: Longer reads mean fewer of them: doubling L to 300 bases halves N to 3.1 x 10^8.
cards.section: Coverage and assembly: two different limits

cards.front: With random read starts and mean coverage C, what fraction of bases is expected to get no read, and why?
cards.back: e^-C. With random starts, the number of reads over a base follows a Poisson distribution with mean C, and e^-C is its zero class.
cards.quote: with random starts, the number of reads over a base follows a Poisson distribution with mean C.
cards.section: Coverage and assembly: two different limits

cards.front: A 5-megabase genome is sequenced at 2-fold mean coverage with random starts. About how many bases get no read?
cards.back: About 680 kilobases. Unread fraction is e^-2 = 0.135 (e^-1 is 0.37, squared). 0.135 x 5,000,000 is about 677,000 bases.
cards.quote: At C = 3: e^-3 is about 0.37 × 0.37 × 0.37, about 0.05 (0.0498 on a calculator).
cards.section: Coverage and assembly: two different limits

cards.front: Why do more reads fix random sampling gaps but not a repeat longer than the reads?
cards.back: More reads add coverage but no new span. For an exact repeat, reads that span it, with unique sequence on each side, place it.
cards.quote: More reads fill sampling gaps but add no new span; reads that span a repeat place it.
cards.section: Coverage and assembly: two different limits

cards.front: A genome has two identical 3-kilobase repeats at different loci. Reads of 150 bases at high depth and reads of 8 kilobases are available. Which can place each copy, and why?
cards.back: The 8-kilobase reads can. One can hold a whole copy plus unique flank on both sides, pinning it. A 150-base read inside the repeat fits either copy equally well.
cards.quote: A 15-kilobase read can hold one whole copy plus several kilobases of unique sequence on each side, pinning that copy in place.
cards.section: Coverage and assembly: two different limits

cards.front: A lab raises short-read coverage from 30-fold to 60-fold hoping to close a gap at two identical 6-kilobase repeats. Predict the result, using what limits each kind of gap.
cards.back: The repeat gap stays. Random sampling gaps are already negligible at 30-fold, and more reads add no new span. The repeat needs reads that cross it. Rule: reads that span a repeat place it.
cards.quote: No 150-base read, and no pair from a 400-base fragment, reaches from unique sequence on one side across the repeat to its far edge.
cards.section: Coverage and assembly: two different limits

cards.front: What did the consortium's 2004 finished human sequence still lack?
cards.back: It still had 341 gaps, many associated with segmental duplications. Centromeres and other heterochromatin were not part of its target.
cards.quote: still had 341 gaps, many associated with segmental duplications; centromeres and other heterochromatin were not part of its target.
cards.section: The human reference: gaps, a finished genome and a pangenome

cards.front: What kind of sequence is the GRCh38 reference?
cards.back: A mosaic of DNA clones from several people, not any one person's genome.
cards.quote: a mosaic of DNA clones from several people, not any one person's genome.
cards.section: The human reference: gaps, a finished genome and a pangenome

cards.front: Why could the Telomere-to-Telomere Consortium close the remaining human gaps?
cards.back: CHM13 cells have two nearly identical copies of each chromosome, and PacBio HiFi plus Oxford Nanopore ultra-long reads spanned the large repeats and duplications.
cards.quote: whose two copies of each chromosome are nearly identical, and a combination of PacBio HiFi and Oxford Nanopore ultra-long reads.
cards.section: The human reference: gaps, a finished genome and a pangenome

cards.front: Why is T2T-CHM13 gapless for every chromosome except Y?
cards.back: The CHM13 cell line lacks a Y chromosome. The assembly is 3.055 billion bases.
cards.quote: is 3.055 billion bases and gapless for every chromosome except Y, which CHM13 lacks.
cards.section: The human reference: gaps, a finished genome and a pangenome

cards.front: How is the 2023 draft human pangenome built, and what does it add over GRCh38?
cards.back: It joins 47 people's genomes, each chromosome copy assembled separately, into a graph with each copy as a path. It added 119 million bases of variable euchromatic sequence missing from GRCh38.
cards.quote: 47 people's genomes, each with its two chromosome copies assembled separately, joined into a graph in which each person's copy is a path.
cards.section: The human reference: gaps, a finished genome and a pangenome

cards.front: Distinguish an SNV, a small indel and a structural variant by size.
cards.back: An SNV changes one base. A small indel inserts or deletes a few bases. A structural variant is larger, by a common convention 50 bases or more.
cards.quote: A structural variant is larger, by a common convention 50 bases or more
cards.section: What varies between two genomes, and why the reference matters

cards.front: What is a copy-number variant?
cards.back: A deletion or duplication that changes the number of copies of a segment.
cards.quote: when a deletion or duplication changes the number of copies of a segment, it is a copy-number variant.
cards.section: What varies between two genomes, and why the reference matters

cards.front: Give two ways the choice of reference changes which variants a genome appears to have.
cards.back: Where the reference carries a rare allele, most people look variant. Where sequence is missing from the reference, reads have no correct place to align and go unmapped or land elsewhere.
cards.quote: where a sequence is missing from the reference, reads from it have no correct place to align, so they go unmapped or land on similar sequence elsewhere.
cards.section: What varies between two genomes, and why the reference matters

cards.front: A person carries a 20-kilobase stretch that the reference lacks. Short reads from it are aligned to that reference. What happens to those reads?
cards.back: They go unmapped or land on similar sequence elsewhere. Rule: with no correct place in the reference, reads cannot align properly.
cards.quote: where a sequence is missing from the reference, reads from it have no correct place to align, so they go unmapped or land on similar sequence elsewhere.
cards.section: What varies between two genomes, and why the reference matters

cards.front: By what three kinds of evidence do short reads detect large variants?
cards.back: Depth, since copy number changes the number of reads. Discordant pairs, ends mapping farther apart than expected or in an unexpected orientation. Split reads, one read aligning in two pieces across a junction.
cards.quote: Short reads detect large variants indirectly, from depth (copy number changes the number of reads)
cards.section: What varies between two genomes, and why the reference matters

cards.front: Short reads from a diploid person give 30-fold depth across a chromosome region but 45-fold across one 50-kilobase segment. How many copies does the segment have, and what does that imply?
cards.back: Three copies in total. Two copies give 30-fold, so 45-fold is 1.5 times that. Discordant pairs oriented head to tail at the ends would support a duplication. Rule: copy number changes the number of reads.
cards.quote: Half depth means one copy instead of two: one chromosome has lost the stretch and the other has not, a heterozygous deletion.
cards.section: Predict and design

cards.front: Read pairs from fragments of about 400 bases map with their ends 5.4 kilobases apart across a region. About how much sequence is missing from that chromosome?
cards.back: About 5 kilobases: 5.4 - 0.4 = 5.0 kilobases. The extra distance between the ends is the deleted length.
cards.quote: The discordant pairs give its size: ends that should lie about 400 bases apart map 10.4 kilobases apart
cards.section: Predict and design

cards.front: Short-read data suggest a heterozygous 10-kilobase deletion. Design a PCR test with primers just outside the breakpoints and say what each chromosome gives.
cards.back: The intact chromosome has primers about 10.4 kb apart, too far for a standard short PCR. The deleted one has them a few hundred bases apart, so a short product comes only from the deleted allele; sequence it to read the junction.
cards.quote: on the deleted chromosome they lie a few hundred bases apart, so a short product appears only from the deleted allele; sequence it to read the junction.
cards.section: Predict and design

cards.front: A patient's deletion is called against GRCh38, but many pangenome haplotypes also lack the stretch. How should it be read, and does it imply a health effect?
cards.back: The reference may carry a less common insertion, so the deletion is common. Either way, finding a variant says nothing on its own about any effect on health.
cards.quote: Finding a variant says nothing on its own about any effect on health.
cards.section: Predict and design

cards.front: Why can real sequencing leave more unread bases than the Poisson coverage model predicts?
cards.back: Real libraries cover some regions, such as very GC-rich ones, less evenly than the model assumes.
cards.quote: Real libraries cover some regions, such as very GC-rich ones, less evenly than the Poisson model assumes.
cards.section: Where the ideal coverage model breaks
